topics.title: Why study the interior? Direct sources

learn.hook: The deepest hole humans have ever drilled, the Kola borehole, goes about 12 km down. The earth's radius is 6,370 km. We have barely scratched the skin!
points: Most landforms on the earth's surface are produced by processes operating in the interior (endogenic processes) together with surface processes, so understanding the interior helps explain the surface.
The earth's radius is about 6,370 km. Nobody can reach the centre, and even the deepest drill, at Kola in the Arctic, has reached only about 12 km.
Direct sources give actual materials. Surface rock and rocks from mining: for example, gold mines in South Africa go as deep as 3–4 km.
Deep drilling projects: the Deep Ocean Drilling Project and the Integrated Ocean Drilling Project, plus the Kola superdeep borehole, provide samples from deeper layers.
Volcanic eruptions bring magma from the interior to the surface, where it can be analysed in laboratories. However, it is hard to know the exact depth it came from.

example.q: What fraction of the earth's radius has the deepest drill (12 km) reached? Take the radius as 6,370 km and give a rough percentage.
steps: Fraction = 12 ÷ 6,370.
As a percentage ≈ 0.19%, i.e., less than 0.2% of the radius.
example.answer: Less than 0.2% of the radius, so direct sources tell us very little about the deep interior.

learn.reallife: The Kolar Gold Fields in Karnataka were among the deepest mines in the world, giving geologists rare rock samples from kilometres below the surface.

items.text: The radius of the earth is about ___ km.
The deepest drill, at Kola, has reached about ___ km.

quiz.q: What is the approximate radius of the earth?
quiz.explain: The earth's radius is about 6,370 km (the diameter is about twice that).
quiz.mistake: Confuses radius with diameter or with the depth of the mantle

quiz.q: The deepest drilling, the Kola superdeep borehole in the Russian Arctic, has reached a depth of about:
quiz.explain: The Kola superdeep borehole reached about 12 km.
quiz.mistake: Overestimates how deep humans have drilled

quiz.q: Which of the following is a direct source of information about the earth's interior?
quiz.explain: Volcanoes bring actual material (magma) from inside to the surface for analysis.
quiz.mistake: Thinks meteorites come from inside the earth

quiz.q: What is the main limitation of using volcanic material to study the interior?
options: Volcanoes erupt only under the sea
It is difficult to know the depth from which the magma came
quiz.explain: Lava can be studied in labs, but its exact source depth is hard to determine.
quiz.mistake: Thinks lava cannot be analysed at all

quiz.q: The Deep Ocean Drilling Project and the Integrated Ocean Drilling Project are examples of:
quiz.explain: Drilling brings up actual rock samples, so these are direct sources.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any scientific project is an indirect source

quiz.q: Why do geographers need to understand the earth's interior?
options: Surface landforms are shaped by processes operating in the interior as well as on the surface
quiz.explain: Endogenic forces from the interior build relief, so knowing the interior helps explain landforms.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the interior has no link with surface features

quiz.q: What percentage of the earth's radius (6,370 km) is 637 km?
steps: Percentage = 637 / 6370 × 100
quiz.mistake: Misplaces the decimal point

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Most of our knowledge about the earth's interior comes from indirect sources.
Reason (R): Direct access through mining and drilling is limited to only a few kilometres.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because we can only reach a few km directly, scientists rely mainly on indirect evidence like seismic waves.
quiz.mistake: Believes drilling has reached the deep interior

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Has anyone dug to the centre of the earth? How do we know what's inside?'
teach.praise: Mines, drilling and volcanoes, the direct sources, and still only 12 km deep! Gappu is amazed.
teach.nudge: What are the direct sources, and how deep do they really go?

learn.hook: Doctors see inside you using X-rays without cutting you open. Geologists 'X-ray' the earth using earthquakes, gravity and magnetism.
points: Temperature, pressure and density all increase with depth. Knowing the thickness of the earth and these rates of change, scientists estimate values at different depths.
Meteors (meteorites) that reach the earth are solid bodies made of materials similar to the earth's, formed in the same nebula, so their structure gives clues to the interior.

Gravitation: the force of gravity is greater near the poles and less at the equator, because of the distance from the centre. Observed gravity also varies with the mass of material below. The difference between expected and observed gravity is called a gravity anomaly; it tells us how mass is distributed in the crust.
Magnetic surveys give information about the distribution of magnetic materials in the crust.
Seismic activity (earthquake waves) is the most important indirect source of information about the interior.

example.q: A survey finds gravity at a place is higher than expected. What does this anomaly suggest?
steps: Gravity depends on the mass of material below.
Higher-than-expected gravity means more mass (denser rock) lies beneath.
So the anomaly reveals a concentration of dense material in the crust.
example.answer: Denser or heavier material lies beneath that place.

learn.reallife: The National Geophysical Research Institute in Hyderabad uses gravity and magnetic surveys to locate mineral deposits and study India's crust.

quiz.explain: All three increase as we go deeper.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

quiz.explain: Uneven distribution of mass below the surface makes gravity vary, causing anomalies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gravity is equal everywhere

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If we can't dig deep, how else can scientists learn about the inside of the earth?'
teach.praise: Seismic waves, gravity anomaly, meteorites and magnetism, the earth's X-ray kit! Gappu loves it.
teach.nudge: Name the indirect sources, and tell Gappu which one is the most important.

topics.title: Earthquakes: focus, epicentre and the seismograph

learn.hook: On 26 January 2001, as India celebrated Republic Day, the ground in Kachchh, Gujarat, began to shake violently. What had happened kilometres below?
points: An earthquake is the shaking of the earth caused by a release of energy, which generates waves that travel in all directions.

The energy is released along a fault, a sharp break in crustal rocks. Rocks along a fault tend to move in opposite directions; friction locks them until the stress overcomes it, and the blocks suddenly shift, releasing energy.
The point inside the earth where the energy is released is the focus, also called the hypocentre.
The epicentre is the point on the surface nearest to the focus (directly above it). It is the first place to experience the waves.
Earthquake waves reaching the surface are recorded by an instrument called a seismograph.

example.q: An earthquake's focus is 20 km below a village. Which place is the epicentre and which feels the waves first?
steps: The focus is the point of energy release, 20 km underground.
The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus.
Here, the village directly above is the epicentre.
The epicentre is the first point on the surface to experience the waves.
example.answer: The village directly above the focus is the epicentre and feels the waves first.

learn.reallife: The National Center for Seismology, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, runs a network of seismographs across India and reports the epicentre of every significant earthquake.

games.title: How an earthquake happens
items: Stress builds up along a fault
Friction holds the rock blocks locked
Stress overcomes friction; blocks move suddenly
Energy is released at the focus
Waves travel in all directions and reach the epicentre

games.title: Earthquake vocabulary

quiz.q: The point inside the earth where an earthquake's energy is released is called the:
quiz.explain: The focus (hypocentre) is where the energy is released.
quiz.mistake: Confuses focus with epicentre

quiz.q: The epicentre of an earthquake is:

The point where the waves end

quiz.explain: The epicentre is on the surface, directly above the focus, and feels the waves first.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the epicentre is underground

quiz.q: Another name for the focus of an earthquake is:
quiz.explain: Focus and hypocentre mean the same thing.
quiz.mistake: Assumes 'hypo-' and 'epi-' refer to the same point

quiz.q: Earthquakes generally occur along:

quiz.explain: Energy is released when rock blocks along a fault overcome friction and slip.
quiz.mistake: Links earthquakes with surface features

quiz.q: Which place on the surface is the first to experience earthquake waves?
options: The opposite side of the earth
quiz.explain: The epicentre is nearest to the focus, so waves reach it first.
quiz.mistake: Thinks distant places feel waves at the same time

quiz.q: The instrument that records earthquake waves is the:
quiz.explain: A seismograph records the waves that reach the surface.
quiz.mistake: Picks a weather instrument

quiz.q: Why does energy build up before an earthquake along a fault?
options: Friction locks the rock blocks while stress keeps increasing
quiz.explain: Rocks try to move but friction holds them; when stress exceeds friction, they slip suddenly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks earthquakes are caused by surface heating

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Earthquake waves travel only upwards from the focus to the epicentre.
Reason (R): The energy released at the focus spreads outward through the surrounding rocks.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: earthquake waves travel in all directions from the focus, not just upwards. R is true, and it is the reason the waves spread everywhere.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the waves move only to the epicentre because it feels them first

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What's the difference between the focus and the epicentre? They sound the same!'
teach.praise: Focus inside, epicentre above, energy from a fault, recorded by a seismograph. Gappu feels the ground steady now!
teach.nudge: Explain to Gappu where the focus and epicentre are, and why earthquakes happen.

topics.title: Earthquake waves: P, S and surface waves

learn.hook: Within seconds of a quake, three messengers race out. The first is fast but gentle, the second shakes harder, and the last is the one that knocks down buildings.
points: Earthquake waves are of two types: body waves and surface waves. Body waves are generated by the release of energy at the focus and move through the body of the earth. Body waves interact with surface rocks to generate surface waves.

P-waves (primary waves) are the fastest and first to arrive. They are similar to sound waves, travel through gaseous, liquid and solid materials, and vibrate parallel to the direction of the wave, causing compression and rarefaction (squeezing and stretching).

S-waves (secondary waves) arrive after a time lag and travel only through solid materials. Their vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation in the vertical plane, creating troughs and crests.
Surface waves are the last to be recorded on the seismograph and are the most destructive: they cause displacement of rocks and the collapse of structures.

The velocity of waves changes as they pass through materials of different density (denser material, higher velocity). Their direction also changes as they reflect or refract at boundaries between layers.

example.q: A seismograph records three wave arrivals: first a fast, weak one; then a stronger one; finally a slow, very damaging one. Name each.
steps: The first to arrive are always the fastest: P-waves.
Next, after a time lag: S-waves.
Last and most destructive: surface waves.

learn.reallife: Earthquake early-warning apps use the head start of fast P-waves to send alerts a few seconds before the damaging waves arrive, enough time to stop metro trains or move away from glass.

games.title: P-wave or S-wave?
items: Vibrations perpendicular to direction of travel

quiz.q: Which earthquake waves can travel through solid, liquid and gaseous materials?
quiz.explain: P-waves are like sound waves and can pass through all three states of matter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks S-waves can also pass through liquids

quiz.q: S-waves can travel only through:
quiz.explain: S-waves cannot pass through liquids or gases; they travel only through solids.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the properties of P and S waves

quiz.q: Which waves are the most destructive?
quiz.explain: Surface waves cause rock displacement and collapse of structures.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the fastest waves cause the most damage

quiz.q: In P-waves, the vibration of particles is:
options: Parallel to the direction of the wave
Perpendicular to the direction of the wave
quiz.explain: P-waves vibrate along the direction of travel, causing compression and rarefaction.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the vibration directions of P and S waves

quiz.q: Waves that are generated when body waves interact with surface rocks are called:
quiz.explain: Body waves interacting with surface rocks produce surface waves.
quiz.mistake: Thinks surface waves start at the focus

quiz.q: S-waves create troughs and crests in the material because:
options: Their vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation
They are reflected at the surface only
quiz.explain: Up-and-down vibrations at right angles to travel produce crests and troughs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks crests come from compression

quiz.q: What happens to the velocity of earthquake waves when they pass into denser material?
quiz.explain: Wave velocity depends on density; it changes at boundaries, and the waves also bend (refract) or reflect.
quiz.mistake: Thinks waves move at the same speed through all layers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): P-waves are recorded first on a seismograph.
Reason (R): P-waves are the fastest earthquake waves.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Being the fastest, P-waves arrive first at any station.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the first arrival is the strongest

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Earthquakes send out different waves? What are they and how are they different?'
teach.praise: Fast P, solid-only S, and destructive surface waves. Gappu's seismograph is buzzing!
teach.nudge: Which waves are fastest, which pass only through solids, and which do the most damage?

topics.title: Shadow zones and what they reveal

learn.hook: After a big quake, some seismographs around the world record nothing at all. That 'silence' told scientists the earth has a liquid outer core.
points: P-waves make material squeeze and stretch along their path; S-waves make it vibrate up and down at right angles to their path (as drawn in NCERT's diagram).
A shadow zone is an area on the surface where earthquake waves are not recorded.
Seismographs within 105° of the epicentre record both P- and S-waves.
Seismographs beyond 145° record P-waves but not S-waves. The zone between 105° and 145° is the shadow zone for both types of waves.

The entire area beyond 105° receives no S-waves, so the S-wave shadow zone is much larger: a little over 40% of the earth's surface. Since S-waves cannot pass through liquids, this shows that the outer core is liquid.

example.q: Three stations are 80°, 120° and 160° from an epicentre. Which waves does each record?
steps: 80° is within 105° → both P and S waves.
120° lies between 105° and 145° → shadow zone for both; no direct P or S waves.
160° is beyond 145° → P-waves only (no S-waves).
example.answer: 80°: P and S; 120°: neither; 160°: P only.

learn.reallife: A strong quake in Japan is recorded with both P and S waves at Indian stations, but stations on the far side of the globe receive no S-waves, a daily reminder of the liquid outer core.

games.title: Shadow zone facts

P-waves are not recorded in this band.
S-waves are recorded at stations beyond 145°.
No S-waves reach any station beyond 105°.
The S-wave shadow zone covers a little over 40% of the earth's surface.
It is much larger than the P-wave shadow zone.
The S-wave shadow zone shows that the inner core is liquid.
It shows the outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid.
The S-wave shadow zone is smaller than the P-wave shadow zone.
The S-wave shadow zone is much larger.

quiz.explain: Within 105°, both P and S waves are recorded.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 145° limit instead

quiz.q: The zone between 105° and 145° from the epicentre is the shadow zone for:
quiz.explain: Neither P nor S waves are recorded directly in this band.
quiz.mistake: Thinks this band receives S-waves

quiz.q: Stations beyond 145° from the epicentre record:
quiz.explain: P-waves reach beyond 145° after passing through the core; S-waves do not.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the whole far side is silent

quiz.q: The S-wave shadow zone covers about how much of the earth's surface?
quiz.explain: The S-wave shadow zone is a little over 40% of the earth's surface.
quiz.mistake: Guesses an even split

quiz.q: The S-wave shadow zone provides evidence that:
quiz.explain: S-waves cannot pass through liquid; their absence beyond 105° shows the outer core is liquid.
quiz.mistake: Assigns the liquid state to the inner core

quiz.q: A shadow zone is:
options: An area of darkness during an eclipse
An area where earthquake waves are not recorded
quiz.explain: It is the region on the surface that does not receive (direct) earthquake waves.

Inner limit = 105°
quiz.mistake: Adds the two limits

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The shadow zone of S-waves is larger than that of P-waves.
Reason (R): S-waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core, so no S-waves reach any point beyond 105°.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because the liquid outer core blocks S-waves, the entire area beyond 105° is their shadow zone, much larger than the P-wave band.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both waves behave the same in the core

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is a shadow zone, and how does it prove anything about the core?'
teach.praise: 105° and 145°, and the missing S-waves prove a liquid outer core. Gappu is impressed!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the key angles and what the S-wave shadow zone proves.

learn.hook: Not every tremor comes from moving plates. Some come from volcanoes, some from collapsing mines, some from bombs and some even from giant dams.
points: Tectonic earthquakes are the most common. They are caused by the sliding of rocks along a fault plane.
Volcanic earthquakes are a special class of tectonic earthquake, confined to areas of active volcanoes.
Collapse earthquakes are minor tremors that occur in areas of intense mining when the roofs of underground mines collapse.
Explosion earthquakes are tremors caused by the explosion of chemical or nuclear devices.
Reservoir induced earthquakes occur in areas of large reservoirs (behind big dams).

example.q: Classify: (a) tremors near the Koyna dam reservoir in Maharashtra; (b) ground shaking during an underground nuclear test; (c) the 2001 Bhuj earthquake caused by fault movement.
steps: (a) Linked to a large reservoir → reservoir induced earthquake.
(b) Caused by an explosion → explosion earthquake.
(c) Caused by sliding of rocks along a fault → tectonic earthquake.

learn.reallife: The 1967 Koyna earthquake in Maharashtra is a famous case studied worldwide as a reservoir-linked earthquake.

learn.hook: Two people describe the same earthquake: one says 'magnitude 7', the other says 'intensity X'. Both are right, because they measure different things.
points: The magnitude scale, known as the Richter scale, measures the energy released during an earthquake. It is expressed in absolute numbers, 0–10.
The intensity scale, named after Mercalli, an Italian seismologist, measures the visible damage caused by the event. It ranges from 1 to 12.
Magnitude is one value for an earthquake (energy at the source); intensity varies from place to place depending on distance, ground and buildings.
Higher-magnitude earthquakes are rare: quakes of magnitude 8+ occur about once in 1–2 years, while tiny ones occur almost every minute.
Indian case: the Bhuj (Kachchh, Gujarat) earthquake of 26 January 2001 caused heavy loss of life and property.

example.q: An earthquake damages old buildings badly in town X near the epicentre and only rattles windows in town Y far away. Which value is the same for both towns and which differs?
steps: Magnitude measures energy released at the source, so it is a single value for the earthquake.
Intensity measures damage seen at a place, so it is higher in X and lower in Y.
example.answer: Magnitude is the same; intensity differs (higher in X).

learn.reallife: After a quake, the National Center for Seismology reports the magnitude; damage surveys by the state disaster authority describe the intensity in each district.

items: The Mercalli scale measures the energy released by an earthquake.
Mercalli measures intensity (damage); Richter measures energy.
Earthquakes of magnitude 8 or more are quite rare.
They occur about once in 1–2 years.
Tiny earthquakes occur almost every minute.
The intensity of an earthquake is the same everywhere.
Intensity varies with distance and local conditions.
The Bhuj earthquake struck on 26 January 2001.

quiz.q: The Richter scale measures the:
quiz.explain: The Richter (magnitude) scale measures energy released, expressed as 0–10.

quiz.q: The Mercalli scale ranges from:
quiz.explain: The intensity (Mercalli) scale has values from 1 to 12.

quiz.q: The intensity of an earthquake refers to:

quiz.q: How often do earthquakes of magnitude 8 or more occur, roughly?
quiz.explain: Large 8+ quakes are rare, about once in 1–2 years; tiny ones occur almost every minute.

quiz.explain: The Bhuj earthquake struck Kachchh district of Gujarat on 26 January 2001.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An earthquake has only one magnitude value.
Reason (R): Magnitude measures the visible damage at different places.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: magnitude is a single value for the energy released. R is false: visible damage is intensity, not magnitude.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the definitions of magnitude and intensity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What's the difference between magnitude and intensity? And how are they measured?'
teach.praise: Richter for energy, Mercalli for damage, and big quakes are rare. Gappu is a mini-seismologist!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu what each scale measures and its range.

learn.hook: In an earthquake, it is mostly falling buildings, fires and floods, not the shaking itself, that hurt people.
points: Earthquakes are a natural hazard. Immediate hazard-causing effects include: ground shaking, differential ground settlement, land and mud slides, soil liquefaction, ground lurching and avalanches.
Other effects: ground displacement, floods from dam and levee failures, and fires.
Further effects: structural collapse, falling objects and tsunami.
The first six effects (ground shaking to avalanches) have some bearing on landforms, while the others are effects of immediate concern to life and property.
A tsunami occurs only if the epicentre is below oceanic waters and the magnitude is sufficiently high.

example.q: Sort these effects into 'bearing on landforms' or 'immediate concern to life and property': soil liquefaction, fires, avalanches, falling objects.
steps: NCERT lists 12 effects; the first six (ground shaking, differential settlement, land/mud slides, soil liquefaction, ground lurching, avalanches) affect landforms.
Soil liquefaction and avalanches → landforms.
Fires and falling objects are among the remaining six → life and property.
example.answer: Landforms: soil liquefaction, avalanches. Life and property: fires, falling objects.

learn.reallife: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) campaigns on 'Drop, Cover and Hold' because falling objects and collapsing structures are the main killers in quakes.

topics.title: Structure of the earth: crust and mantle

learn.hook: If the earth were an apple, the crust would be thinner than its skin, yet it holds every mountain, ocean and city.
points: The crust is the outermost solid part of the earth. It is brittle in nature. Its thickness varies: about 5 km under the oceans, about 30 km on continents, and as much as 70 km under major mountain systems such as the Himalaya.
The crust is made up of rocks with a density of about 3 g/cm³; the rock of the oceanic crust is basalt.
The mantle extends from the Moho discontinuity (the crust–mantle boundary) to a depth of 2,900 km.
The upper portion of the mantle is the asthenosphere ('astheno' = weak), extending up to about 400 km. It is the main source of magma and has a higher density than the crust (about 3.4 g/cm³).
The crust and the uppermost part of the mantle together form the lithosphere, 10–200 km thick. The lower mantle, beyond the asthenosphere, is in a solid state.

example.q: How much thicker is the continental crust under the Himalaya (70 km) than the oceanic crust (5 km)?
steps: Difference = 70 − 5 = 65 km.
example.answer: 65 km thicker, or 14 times as thick.

learn.reallife: The Himalaya's thick crustal root (up to about 70 km) is part of why the region is so geologically active and earthquake-prone.

topics.title: The core and the full picture of the interior

learn.hook: At the centre of the earth, about 6,300 km down, material is about 13 times as dense as water. It is a giant ball of metal.
points: The core–mantle boundary lies at a depth of 2,900 km (the Gutenberg discontinuity).
The outer core is in a liquid state; the inner core is in a solid state.
Density is around 5 g/cm³ at the mantle–core boundary and around 13 g/cm³ at the centre of the earth (at about 6,300 km).
The core is made of very heavy material, mostly nickel and iron. It is sometimes called the 'nife' layer (Ni + Fe).
Diagram practice: label crust, Moho discontinuity, upper mantle (asthenosphere), lower mantle, Gutenberg discontinuity at 2,900 km, liquid outer core and solid inner core.

example.q: Why is the core called the 'nife' layer?
steps: The core is made mostly of very heavy materials.
These are nickel (chemical symbol Ni) and iron (Fe).
Ni + Fe → 'nife'.
example.answer: Because it is made mostly of nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe).

learn.reallife: The earth's magnetic field, which compasses and migrating birds use, is linked to the movement of molten iron in the liquid outer core.

quiz.explain: The core begins at 2,900 km depth.

quiz.explain: The core is the 'nife' layer: nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe).

quiz.explain: The outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A

quiz.explain: Both are true, but the liquid outer core does not explain why the inner core is solid; that is due to the enormous pressure at the centre.

topics.title: Volcanoes, volcanic materials and shield volcanoes

learn.hook: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only active volcano. Its smoke and lava are messages sent up from the asthenosphere.
points: A volcano is a place where gases, ashes and/or molten rock material (lava) escape to the ground.
A volcano is called active if these materials are being released or have been released in the recent past.
Molten rock in the upper mantle (asthenosphere) is called magma. Once it starts moving towards the crust or reaches the surface, it is called lava.

Materials that reach the ground include lava flows, pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs, ash and dust, and gases such as nitrogen compounds, sulphur compounds and minor amounts of chlorine, hydrogen and argon.

Shield volcanoes are the largest of all volcanoes (barring basalt flows), e.g. the Hawaiian volcanoes. They are mostly basalt, a lava that is very fluid when erupted, so they are not steep. They have low explosivity, but become explosive if water gets into the vent. Lava fountains can build a cinder cone at the top.

example.q: A volcano has gentle slopes, is built of fluid basaltic lava and erupts quietly. Identify its type and explain the gentle slope.
steps: Gentle slopes + basalt + quiet eruption → shield volcano.
Basaltic lava is very fluid (low viscosity).
Fluid lava flows far before cooling, so it builds a broad, gently sloping shape.
example.answer: Shield volcano; its fluid basaltic lava spreads widely, giving gentle slopes.

learn.reallife: Barren Island, about 135 km north-east of Port Blair, has erupted several times in recent decades and is monitored by Indian scientists.

quiz.q: When does a shield volcano become explosive?
options: When water gets into the vent
When it is in the tropics

Reason (R): Their basaltic lava is highly viscous.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: basaltic lava is very fluid (low viscosity), which lets gases escape easily.
quiz.mistake: Confuses fluid basalt with viscous lava

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What comes out of a volcano? And why are some volcanoes so flat and wide?'

topics.title: Composite volcanoes, calderas, flood basalts and mid-ocean ridges

learn.hook: Some volcanoes build tall cones, some blow themselves apart, and some flood whole regions. The Deccan Traps of Maharashtra are lava floods frozen in stone.
points: Composite volcanoes erupt cooler and more viscous lavas than basalt and often cause explosive eruptions. Large quantities of pyroclastic material and ash accumulate near the vent, forming layers; that layering gives them the name composite.

Calderas are the most explosive volcanoes. They are so explosive that they collapse on themselves instead of building tall structures; the collapsed depressions are calderas. Their explosiveness shows that the magma chamber is huge and close to the surface.
Flood basalt provinces: highly fluid lava flows for long distances, covering thousands of sq km. Some flows are more than 50 m thick, and individual flows extend for hundreds of km.
The Deccan Traps of India, which now cover most of the Maharashtra plateau, are a much larger flood basalt province; they once covered an even larger area.
Mid-ocean ridge volcanoes occur in the oceans. A system of mid-ocean ridges more than 70,000 km long runs through all the ocean basins, and its central portion has frequent eruptions.

example.q: Identify the volcano type: (a) a huge depression formed when a volcano collapses after a violent eruption; (b) cones with alternate layers of lava and ash; (c) thick lava sheets covering the Maharashtra plateau.
steps: (a) Collapse into a depression → caldera.
(b) Layers of lava and pyroclastic material → composite volcano.
(c) Extensive thick flows of fluid lava → flood basalt province (Deccan Traps).
example.answer: (a) Caldera; (b) Composite volcano; (c) Flood basalt province.

learn.reallife: The flat-topped hills of the Western Ghats near Mahabaleshwar and Lonavala are stacked layers of Deccan basalt, like a giant stone layer cake.

quiz.q: The Deccan Traps of India are an example of:
quiz.explain: The Deccan Traps are thick, extensive basalt flows covering most of the Maharashtra plateau.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Deccan Traps are a single volcano

It is located on a mid-ocean ridge

options: They have both land and sea vents

quiz.explain: Layering of lava, ash and pyroclastic material near the vent gives them their composite structure.

steps: Total thickness = 1,000 m

quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Calderas do not usually build tall volcanic structures.
Reason (R): They are so explosive that they tend to collapse on themselves.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The violent eruption empties the chamber, the top collapses, and a depression forms instead of a cone.
quiz.mistake: Thinks explosive volcanoes always build the tallest cones

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Are all volcanoes the same cone shape? What about the Deccan Traps?'
teach.praise: Composite cones, collapsing calderas, flood basalts and ocean ridges. Gappu is a volcano expert now!
teach.nudge: Describe composite volcanoes and calderas, and say what the Deccan Traps are.

learn.hook: Not all lava reaches the surface. Some cools underground into domes, saucers and walls, which erosion later uncovers, like the granite domes of Karnataka.
points: Lava that cools on the surface forms volcanic rocks; lava that cools within the crust forms plutonic rocks. Forms cooled inside the crust are called intrusive forms.

Batholiths: large bodies of magma that cool deep in the crust as large domes. They are granitic, cover large areas, can be several km deep, and appear on the surface only after denudation removes the overlying material. They are the cooled portions of magma chambers.

Lacoliths: large dome-shaped intrusive bodies with a level base, connected by a pipe-like conduit from below. The Karnataka plateau is dotted with granite domal hills, mostly now exfoliated, that are examples of lacoliths or batholiths.

Lapolith: a saucer-shaped body, concave to the sky. Phacolith: a wavy mass of intrusive rock found at the base of synclines or the top of anticlines in folded igneous country, with a conduit to a magma chamber below.

Sills and sheets are near-horizontal intrusive bodies: thick ones are sills, thin ones are sheets. Dykes are wall-like structures formed when lava solidifies almost perpendicular to the ground in cracks; they are the most common intrusive forms in western Maharashtra and are considered the feeders of the Deccan Traps.

example.q: A geologist finds a vertical, wall-like band of basalt cutting across horizontal rock layers in western Maharashtra. Name it and state its significance.
steps: A vertical wall-like intrusion that cuts across layers is a dyke.
Dykes are the most common intrusive forms in western Maharashtra.
They are considered the feeders (channels) for the lava eruptions that built the Deccan Traps.
example.answer: A dyke, a feeder for the Deccan Trap eruptions.

learn.reallife: The rounded granite hills around Bengaluru and Hampi in Karnataka are exfoliated domes linked with batholiths and lacoliths, now popular rock-climbing spots.

Reason (R): Batholiths are large granitic bodies that cooled deep inside the crust.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
